## Methods

Cell culture
Rat and human NPCs were obtained from NP tissues by collagenase digestion for 4 h89. Rat AFCs were obtained from annulus fibrosus tissues by collagenase and hyaluronidase digestion for 1.5 h90. Rat EPCs were obtained from endplate cartilage tissues by collagenase digestion for 6 h91. Rat NP tissues, annulus fibrosus tissues and endplate cartilage tissues were macroscopically isolated from 4-week-old male Sprague–Dawley rats. Rat NPCs, AFCs, and EPCs were seeded with media changed every 72 h, passaged when the confluence reached 80%, and utilized before passage 2. Human NP tissues were obtained from human participants undergoing spinal surgery for vertebral fractures or IVDD. Cultures of primary human NPCs were maintained under standard conditions (5% CO2 and 37°C), and the medium was changed every 72 h. The human NPCs were passaged on the sixth day. To evaluate the impact of in vitro culture on the phenotypic changes in degenerated human NPCs, cell samples were collected every other day from day 1 to day 9 of culture. These samples were subsequently used for gene and protein analysis of NPC phenotypic markers. The use of patient samples was approved by the Ethics Committee of Sir Run Run Shaw Hospital. Informed consent was obtained from all the patients involved in the study. The cells were seeded in a humidified incubator and cultured in Dulbecco’s modified Eagle medium (DMEM), supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (Gibco). For plasmid transfection, we used IH-NPCs (iCell Bioscience, Inc., iCell-0028a), which were cultured in specialized culture medium (iCell Bioscience, Inc.).

NTU and NM-NTU preparation
Chloroplasts were isolated from fresh spinach leaves using differential centrifugation and Percoll density gradient centrifugation, and then suspended in a hypotonic lysis buffer to obtain thylakoids19,92. The thylakoids were extruded sequentially through polycarbonate membranes with pore sizes of 800-, 400-, 200-, and 100-nm to obtain NTUs. The NPC membranes were isolated from disrupted NPCs by differential centrifugation19 and suspended in water at a concentration of 2 mg mL−1. Subsequently, the NPC membrane solution was mixed with an equal volume of the NTUs and allowed to stand for 30 min. Next, the mixed solution was filtered through 1000-, 400-, and 200-nm polycarbonate membranes using an Avanti mini extruder. NM-NTUs were obtained through centrifugation at 10,000 × g for 5 min and were resuspended for further use. The chlorophyll content was determined by spectrophotometric analysis93. To evaluate the encapsulation efficiency of the NTUs by NM, we used nanoFCM. NTUs were stained with Star Red and detected in the PC5 channel. The NMs were labeled with a FITC-conjugated marker, allowing their specific detection in the FITC channel. Different NTU and NM protein ratios (ranging from 1:10 to 1:200) were tested. Events that were positive for both FITC and PC5 (FITC+/PC5+) were classified as NMs successfully loaded with NTUs, whereas events that were positive for FITC but negative for PC5 (FITC+/PC5-) were categorized as empty NMs. Events that were positive for PC5 but negative for FITC (FITC-/PC5+) were categorized as free NTUs. NTU and NM-NTU morphologies were observed using cryo-TEM (200 kV, FEI Tecnai G2 F20). The size and surface zeta potential of the nanoparticles were determined via dynamic light scattering using a Malvern Zetasizer Nano ZS49. SDS-PAGE and Coomassie Blue (Beyotime) staining were used to detect proteins in the thylakoids, NTUs, NPC membranes, and NM-NTUs.

Antibodies
The following antibodies were used for western blotting: CHOP (Proteintech, 15204-1-AP, 1:1,500); IRE1 (Proteintech, 27528-1-AP, 1:1,500); ATF6 (Proteintech, 66563-1-Ig, 1:10,000); ATF4 (Proteintech, 60035-1-Ig, 1:2000)；β-actin (Proteintech, 20536-1-AP, 1:5000).

For immunofluorescence analysis, the following antibodies were used: KRT19 (Proteintech, 10712-1-AP, 1:200), CD24 (Proteintech, 10600-1-AP, 1:200), CHOP (Proteintech, 15204-1-AP, 1:100); ATF4 (Proteintech, 60035-1-Ig, 1:200); ColII (Proteintech, 28459-1-AP, 1:800); aggrecan (Proteintech, 13880-1-AP, 1:200); MMP13 (Proteintech, 18165-1-AP, 1:200); ADAMTS-5 (Affinity Biosciences, DF13268, 1:200); TOMM20 (Abcam, ab56783, 1:200); Calnexin (Proteintech, 10427-2-AP, 1:200).

Cell viability assay
Human NPC viability was evaluated using two independent assays: the MTT assay (Beyotime) and the live/dead staining assay (Beyotime). An MTT assay was performed to measure cellular metabolic activity. Briefly, yellow, water-soluble MTT tetrazolium salt was added to the cell culture. The absorbance at 570 nm was measured spectrophotometrically. A live/dead staining assay was used to simultaneously distinguish viable cells from nonviable cells on the basis of membrane integrity. Cells were stained with a combination of calcein AM and propidium iodide. Images were acquired using a laser confocal microscope (LCM, Nikon), and the percentages of live and dead cells were quantified using Fiji/ImageJ software. Rat NPCs were incubated with NTU or NM-NTUs (0.5 μg mL−1 for chlorophyll) for 24 h. A CCK-8 assay was performed to determine cell viability (Dojindo).

Cellular uptake of NM-NTUs
We evaluated the cellular uptake of the NM-NTUs by rat AFCs, EPCs and NPCs. Briefly, cells were incubated with a medium containing NM-NTUs (DiI labeled NTUs, 0.5 μg mL−1 for chlorophyll) for 6 h, followed by washing, fixation with 4% formalin, and DAPI staining. The cells were imaged and analyzed using an LCM (Nikon). NPCs were cultured, labeled with DiI, and treated with a medium containing NM-NTUs (DiO labeled NM, 0.5 μg mL−1 for chlorophyll) for 1 h to detect the membrane fusion ability of NM-NTUs. Samples were fixed with 4% formalin, stained with DAPI, and photographed using an LCM (Nikon).

Intracellular trafficking of NTUs in NPCs
NTUs or NM-NTUs (DiI labeled NTUs, 0.5 μg mL−1 for chlorophyll) were co-cultured with rat NPCs for 6 h, and lysosomes were labeled with lysoTracker Green (Beyotime) to investigate the co-localization of NTUs and lysosomes in cells. Subsequently, cells were fixed with 4% formalin and stained with DAPI; images were captured using an LCM (Nikon). Next, Mander’s overlap coefficients of lysosomes and NTUs were analyzed using Fiji/ImageJ (JACoP plugin). Colocalization studies were performed to determine the intracellular distribution of internalized NM-NTUs. After rat NPCs were incubated with NM-NTUsDiI (NTUs labeled with DiI) for 6 h, the samples were stained for specific cellular structures, including the endoplasmic reticulum (ER-Tracker Green, Beyotime), mitochondria (Mito-Tracker Green, Beyotime), Golgi apparatus (Golgi-Tracker Green, Beyotime), actin filaments (Actin-Tracker Green, Beyotime), and microtubules (Tubulin-Tracker Green, Beyotime). Confocal microscopy images were acquired, and colocalization was quantitatively analyzed using Mander’s overlap coefficients. The Mander’s coefficients (M1) quantify the fraction of the signal intensity of NTUs that colocalizes with lysosomes relative to the total signal intensity of NTUs.

To visualize MERCS, IH-NPCs were transfected with SPLICSMt-ER Short P2A (Addgene plasmid #164108) encoding the mitochondrial outer membrane-targeted OMM-GFP1-10 and the endoplasmic reticulum-targeted short protein GFPβ11 (1 μg plasmid of a 35 mm glass bottom dish) using Lipofectamine 3000, strictly following the manufacturer’s protocol. At 36–48 h post-transfection, the cells were treated with DiI-labeled NM-NTUs for 6 h. After treatment, the cells were imaged using confocal microscopy. The reconstituted GFP signal, which indicates close-range (~8–10 nm) MERCS, and the DiI signal (NTUs) were captured. Colocalization between NTUs and MERCS puncta was quantitatively analyzed using the JACoP plugin in Fiji/ImageJ software, with the results expressed as the Mander’s coefficient (M1) representing the fraction of the NTU signal overlapping with MERCS.

Effects of NM-NTUs on cell metabolism
Rat NPCs were treated with IL-1β (20 ng mL−1) for 24 h and incubated with NM-NTUs (0.5 μg mL−1 for chlorophyll) for 6 h, with or without red light irradiation (from light-emitting diodes, peaking at 630 nm at an intensity of 80 μmol photons m−2 s−1, 30 min). The NPCs were incubated with the corresponding antibodies for immunofluorescence staining. Images were captured using an LCM (Nikon, Tokyo, Japan). Images were analyzed and fluorescence intensity was measured using the Fiji/ImageJ software. The intracellular ATP concentration was analyzed using an ATP assay kit (Beyotime). To evaluate the ATP production efficiency of the NM-NTU at different concentrations, we measured ATP levels under NM-NTU concentrations ranging from 0.125 to 2 μg mL−1 for chlorophyll. Similarly, ATP production under varying light conditions (10.3–108.1 μmol photons m−² s−¹) was also assessed. To specifically quantify ATP production from NM-NTUs, we inhibited mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation and glycolysis using rotenone (500 nM) and 2-DG (10 mM). After the NM-NTUs were subjected to light treatment for 30 min, ATP levels were measured using an ATP assay kit. For intracellular NADPH quantification, cells from each group were lysed and analyzed using an NADPH assay kit (Beyotime) according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

Assessment of endogenous mitochondrial functional recovery
IH-NPCs were transfected with pCMV-Mito-AT1.03 (Beyotime, D2606). Cells were seeded in 6-well plates, and each well was transfected with 1 μg of plasmid using Lipofectamine 3000. At 24–36 h post-transfection, the cells were treated with IL-1β for an additional 24 h. Mitochondrial ATP levels were subsequently quantified by flow cytometry on the basis of the ratio of YFP to CFP fluorescence following NM-NTUs + light treatment.

Quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR)
Total RNA was extracted from the lysed NPCs using the SteadyPure RNA Extraction Kit (Accurate Biology). RNA was reverse-transcribed into cDNA using Evo M-MLV RT Master Mix (Accurate Biology), and qPCR was performed using the Hieff UNICON qPCR SYBR Green Master Mix on a QuantStudioTM 6 Flex Real-Time PCR System (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Target gene sequences are listed in Supplementary Table 2.

Determination of cytoplasmic and mitochondrial Ca2+ concentration
NPCs were loaded with 2 μM Rhod-2/AM (50 min; Yeasen). The cells were then washed and reloaded with 5 μM Fluo-4/AM (30 min; Beyotime)94. Images were recorded using an LCM (Nikon). Image analysis and fluorescence intensity measurements were performed using the Fiji/ImageJ software.

Detection of ER Ca2+ concentration
To investigate the contribution of photosynthetic ATP to ER calcium storage, IH-NPCs were transfected with pCMV G-CEPIA1er (Addgene# 58215), which encodes an ER calcium indicator65. Photosynthetic ATP production in the NM-NTU was inhibited by treatment with 10 μM DCMU. The experimental design included eight treatment groups analyzed at 0, 15, and 30-min time points: control, IL-1β, IL-1β + NM-NTU + dark, and IL-1β + NM-NTU + light, with each condition further divided into subgroups either treated with or without DCMU. Cells were imaged using an LCM (Nikon), and quantitative analysis of fluorescence intensity was performed using Fiji/ImageJ software to assess [Ca2+]ER.

mPTP evaluation
The mPTP of the NPCs was evaluated based on the calcein release assay95 using an mPTP assay kit (Beyotime) and photographed using an LCM (Nikon).

MERCS observation
MERCS structures of the NPCs were observed using TEM (H-9500; Hitachi). MERCS in TEM images were manually analyzed in Fiji/ImageJ. Briefly, the image scale was first set with the Set Scale tool, and the freehand line tool was subsequently used to measure the length of the ER or membrane or the perimeter of the mitochondria. The contact length was defined as the ER membrane length (within 0–100 nm of the mitochondria) divided by the mitochondrial perimeter. Mitochondria and ER architecture in the TEM images were reconstructed graphically using Adobe Illustrator software. Similarly, the MERCS structure of the NPCs was observed by immunostaining the ER and mitochondria with calnexin and TOMM20. To quantify MERCS, we performed colocalization analysis using Fiji/ImageJ plugins (Coloc2 and JACoP) following established methods96. The Mander’s coefficients (M1) quantify the percentage of the signal intensity of mitochondria that colocalizes with the ER relative to the total signal intensity of the mitochondria.

Membrane fluidity detection
The global membrane fluidity of the NPCs was evaluated using a membrane fluidity kit (Abcam), which utilizes fluorescent lipophilic pyrene probes that are incorporated into the cell membrane. The monomeric pyrene probe undergoes excimer formation, shifting its emission from Em 400 nm to Em 470 nm (excitation at 360 nm). Membrane fluidity was quantified by determining the ratio of excimer (Em 470 nm) to monomer (Em 400 nm) fluorescence using a fluorescence microplate reader (BioTek).

Intracellular ROS and mitochondrial membrane potential detection
A ROS assay kit (Beyotime) was used to detect intracellular ROS. The DCFH-DA (Beyotime) fluorescence emission was acquired by flow cytometry or LCM. Furthermore, a JC-1 fluorescent probe (Solarbio) was used to detect mitochondrial membrane potential in NPCs. Image analysis and fluorescence intensity measurement were performed using the Fiji/ImageJ software.

Western blot analysis
NPCs were lysed using RIPA buffer (FDbio). SDS-PAGE gels (FDbio) were used to separate the proteins. Proteins were transferred onto polyvinylidene difluoride membranes (FDbio) after electrophoresis. After blocking with skim milk (FDbio) and incubation with the primary antibody, bands were developed using Horseradish peroxidase-labeled secondary antibodies (Beyotime). Following chemiluminescence detection, bands were visualized using the ChemiDoc Touch imaging system (Bio-Rad).

Transcriptomic and lipidomic study
Human NP tissues and rat NPCs were used for transcriptomic analysis. Briefly, total RNA was extracted using TRIzol reagent, following the manufacturer’s instructions. Sequencing was performed using an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 following the manufacturer’s protocol recommended by the supplier. Genes with a P value < 0.05 and an absolute log(fold changes) ≥ 1 were considered differentially expressed. GSEA was performed using GSEA software (https://www.broadinstitute.org/gsea/). Volcanomaps and other visual analyses were performed using the OmicStudio tools (https://www.omicstudio.cn/tool).

For the lipidomic experiment, the ER from rat NPCs was isolated using an ER isolation kit (Sigma), and sample pretreatment and analysis were conducted. Data analysis and acquisition were primarily performed using a Vanquish Flex UHPLC system (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and a TSQ Altis Plus mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Quantification of lipid species was determined by comparison to the relevant internal standard using Skyline 22.2.0527. All detected lipids were annotated and classified based on the lipid databases (https://www.lipidmaps.org/; http://lipidontology.com/). Metabolites with P < 0.05 and fold change > 10% were considered significant.

TLC analysis
Thin-layer chromatography (TLC) was used for TG quantification97. Specifically, the total lipids in the ER extracts were obtained by suspending the ER in 1 mL of PBS supplemented with 0.1 mM phenylmethylsulphonyl fluoride (PMSF) and 2 mL of chloroform/methanol (2:1 vol/vol) supplemented with 0.01% butylated hydroxytoluene. After centrifugation at 1500 × g for 5 min, the organic phases were collected and dried with nitrogen and resuspended in chloroform. TLC was performed by spotting the total lipid extracts dissolved in chloroform onto 10 cm EMD TLC Silica Gel plates (Labshark) and developing them with hexane/diethyl ether/acetic acid (80:20:2, vol/vol). Lipids were visualized with iodine vapor prior to imaging.

PU-wp-LED assembly
The 220 pF multi-layer ceramic capacitor (221K, 0603) and surface-mount-device (SMD) LED (0805) were soldered on a 2.2 MH SMD power inductor (222, CD43) in parallel. Subsequently, wp-LED was encapsulated in PU and wrapped with poly-wires. The PU-wp-LEDs were detected immediately after assembly using a wireless charging coil (XINKETAI Electronic Co., Ltd.). The light intensity of the device was measured using a spectral illuminance meter (Linshang LS330). A laser power meter (Zhongxi Equipment) was used to measure the efficiency of red light penetrating the annulus fibrosus (3 mm thickness) from the sheep.

Biosafety of PU-wp-LED
To determine the biosafety of PU or PU-wp-LED in vitro, we soaked PU or PU-wp-LED in DMEM for 48 h to obtain the leachate. Subsequently, the NPCs were cultured with the leachate for 24 h. CCK-8 assay (Dojindo) was used to detect cell viability.

Animal models
The animal use protocol was reviewed and approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of the Zhejiang Center of Laboratory Animals. Male Sprague–Dawley rats (12 weeks old) were used for in vivo experiments. The IVDD rat model was established using the needle puncture method98. First, rats were anesthetized with pentobarbital sodium. Subsequently, the IVDD models were established using a 26G needle puncture of the coccyx spaces Co7–8. The needle reached the NP center and was removed after 30 s. Rat were randomly divided into four groups, namely sham surgery (sham), puncture and 5 μL vehicle (Puncture + Vehicle) injection per week, puncture + 5 μL NM-NTUs (20 μg mL−1 for chlorophyll) injection per week without red light irradiation (Puncture + NM-NTUs + dark), and puncture + 5 μL NM-NTU injection (20 μg mL−1 for chlorophyll) per week with red light irradiation for 30 min daily (Puncture + NM-NTUs + light). At week 4 and 8, the rats were euthanized for further evaluation.

Male New Zealand rabbits (6–7 months old) were used for in vivo experiments. The rabbits were anesthetized with pentobarbital sodium and placed in a prone position on a platform. The PU-wp-LEDs were implanted subcutaneously to assess their safety and lighting performance. Briefly, a small incision was made in the dorsal skin of the rabbit, and the subcutaneous tissue was separated using a blunt probe; subsequently, the PU-wp-LED was inserted subcutaneously, and the wound was sutured (PU-wp-LED group). The illumination capability of the PU-wp-LED in vivo was tested immediately after surgery. The sham group underwent a surgical procedure similar to that of the implantation group; however, it did not involve PU-wp-LED implantation (sham group). The body temperature of the rabbits was measured daily for 1 week after implantation, and routine blood tests were performed 2 weeks after implantation. For the intervertebral disc illumination simulation, rabbit spines were exposed using a lateral retroperitoneal approach with aseptic techniques. Next, PU-wp-LED was implanted anterior to the L4/5 disc, fixed to the soft tissue structure with a silk thread, and the incision was closed. The intervertebral disc was punctured using a 20G needle under X-ray guidance to simulate deep NM-NTU injection.

For rabbit IVDD treatment, the rabbits were anesthetized and their spines were exposed. L4/5 IVD were punctured with an 18G needle at a depth of 5 mm, then PU-wp-LED was implanted anterior to the L4/5 disc and fixed to the soft tissue structure with silk thread, and the incision was closed. The following intra-disc injection was via X-ray fluoroscopy guide. Rabbits were randomly divided into 4 groups: sham surgery (sham), puncture and 10 μL vehicle (Puncture + Vehicle) injection per week, puncture + 10 μL NM-NTUs (20 μg mL−1 for chlorophyll) injection per week with PU-wp-LED turn off (Puncture + PU-wp-LED + NM-NTUs + dark), and puncture + 10 μL NM-NTU injection (20 μg mL−1 for chlorophyll) per week with PU-wp-LED turn on for 30 min daily (Puncture + PU-wp-LED + NM-NTUs + light). At week 4 and 8, the rabbits were euthanized for further evaluation. And PU-wp-LED were removed before imaging evaluation. To compare the effects of implantable versus non implantable optical stimulation, the rabbits were randomly assigned to one of four groups: sham surgery (sham), puncture and 10 μL vehicle (Puncture + Vehicle) injection per week, puncture + 10 μL NM-NTUs (20 μg mL−1 for chlorophyll) injection per week with external red light illumination for 30 min daily (Puncture + NM-NTUs + External illumination), and puncture + 10 μL NM-NTU injection (20 μg mL−1 for chlorophyll) per week with PU-wp-LED turn on for 30 min daily (Puncture + NM-NTUs + PU-wp-LED illumination). The PU-wp-LED implants were removed prior to imaging evaluation. All the animals were euthanized at week 8 for subsequent analysis.

In vivo radiological assessment
Magnetic resonance imaging was performed on vertebral samples 4 and 8 weeks postoperatively using a GE Sigma CV/I (1.5 T). The rat caudal vertebral samples were scanned using micro-CT (Skyscan 1275). We defined the regions of interest to cover the upper and lower normal intervertebral spaces. The calculation method for DHI is shown in Supplementary Fig. 14. DHI was calculated using the following equation:
DHI = 2 × (A + B + C) / (D + E + F + G + H + I) (1)
where A, B, and C represent the disc height between adjacent vertebrae; and D, E, F, G, H, and I represent the length of the vertebral bone immediately rostral and caudal to the intervertebral disc. Changes in the DHI were expressed as a percentage (%DHI = measured DHI / Sham group DHI × 100). Fiji/ImageJ software was used to measure the signal intensity on the T2-weighted central images. A CT scan was used to confirm the fixation of the PU-wp-LED anterior to the rabbit intervertebral disc.

Histological analysis
Disc samples were fixed, decalcified, and embedded to obtain the sections. These sections were stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E), Alcian blue, Safranin O-fast green, or Picrosirius red. The disc samples were scored according to the table shown in Supplementary Table 3. Subsequently, the sections were incubated with the corresponding antibodies for immunofluorescence staining. Rat major organs were collected at 8 weeks for systemic toxicity assessment (through H&E staining).

Statistics and reproducibility
Data were presented as mean ± standard deviations. The statistical analysis methods were described in the figure legends. Unpaired two-tailed Student’s or Welch’s t test (two independent groups) and one-way analysis of variance with Tukey’s post hoc test (three or more groups) were used. Ordinal grading system data were analyzed using the Kruskal–Wallis and post-hoc Dunn’s tests. Statistical significance was set at P < 0.05. Statistical analyses were performed using Excel and GraphPad Prism software version 10.0. Particle size analysis, zeta potential, SDS-PAGE, cryo-TEM, Western blot, and in vitro fluorescence imaging experiments were independently repeated three times. H&E staining of major organs in rats were replicated in two independent experiments.

Response: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comment regarding the
causal relationship between lipid unsaturation, membrane fluidity, and MAM formation.
We agree that additional references would strengthen our interpretation. Biomembranes
are materials composed of proteins embedded in a bilayer of lipids. One of the major
factors affecting membrane fluidity is the degree of unsaturation of fatty acid chains
[PMID: 37652754, 28356571]. Saturated lipid acyl chains tend to form nonfluid, tightly
packed gel phases at physiological temperatures, whereas unsaturated lipid acyl chains
fluidize the bilayer [PMID: 29410529]. Membranes rich in unsaturated lipids can adopt
a fluid and disordered phase known as the liquid crystalline phase (Lα). Membranes
that mainly consist of saturated lipids can adopt an ordered and rigid gel phase (Lβ)
[PMID: 37652754]. In summary, tightly packed lipids (saturated lipids) increase
membrane lipid order and make them stiffer, whereas loosely packed lipids (unsaturated
lipids) increase membrane fluidity.
With respect to the connection between membrane fluidity and MAMs, loss of the
p97-UBXD8 complex increases the number of mitochondrial–endoplasmic reticulum
contact sites (MERCS) by reducing membrane lipid unsaturation through the SREBP1-
SCD1 pathway [PMID: 36746962]. UBXD8 KO cells exhibited greater abundances of
PCs, PEs, DGs, and TG lipids with saturated fatty acyl tails, leading to decreased global
membrane fluidity, which in turn resulted in increased MERCS. This aberrant contact
phenotype could be rescued by unsaturated fatty acid supplementation. Ganji et al.
reported that increased membrane saturation/order leading to loss of fluidity might
affect the dynamic association and disassociation between organelles, further leading
to an increase in MERCS [PMID: 36746962].
These studies reveal the connection between lipid unsaturation, membrane fluidity,
and MAM formation.

experiments on NM-NTUsDiI (NTUs labelled with DiI) with organelles (endoplasmic
reticulum, mitochondria, and the Golgi apparatus) and cytoskeletal components (actin

cell through the cytoskeleton; this phenomenon has similarities to previous reports of
cytoskeleton-driven chloroplast movement in plants [PMID: 19620714, 21772030].

Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this comment regarding the
experimental design of the lipidome. Like in Comment-5, in our initial submission, we
inadvertently raised confusion by not clearly specifying that the group labelled “IL-1β
+ NM-NTU” in the ER lipidome experiment actually referred to “IL-1β + NM-NTU +
light”. We deeply apologize for this labelling oversight.
We fully agree that comparing both the IL-1β + NM-NTU + dark and the IL-1β +
NM-NTU + light conditions is essential for clarifying the photodependency of the
effects of the NM-NTU. To address this point, we repeated the lipidomic experiment
and added an “IL-1β + NM-NTU + dark” group. In the new lipidomic results, we
identified 876 metabolites in the ER lipidome, with 392 significantly different
metabolites between the IL-1β + NM-NTU + light group and the IL-1β + NM-NTU +
dark group (Response Figures 9a, 10a). PCA revealed distinct clustering among
samples within groups, with similar metabolite profiles in the control and IL-1β + NM-
NTU + light groups, while both groups clustered separately from the IL-1β and IL-1β
+ NM-NTU + dark groups (Response Figure 9b). Compared with the IL-1β + NM-NTU
+ dark group, the IL-1β + NM-NTU + light group significantly affected Ca2+-dependent
events and lipid metabolism (Response Figures 9c, 10b). Kyoto Encyclopaedia of
Genes and Genomes enrichment analysis revealed that NM-NTU + light treatment
affected pathways related to the biosynthesis of unsaturated fatty acids (Response
Figure 10c).
We subsequently analysed the distribution and changes in ER lipid categories
among the groups. Compared with those in the control group, the triglyceride (TG)
levels were significantly reduced in the IL-1β and IL-1β + NM-NTU + dark groups,
whereas they were restored in the IL-1β + NM-NTU + light treatment group (Response
Figure 9d). The levels of other major ER lipid species (e.g., phosphatidylcholine,
phosphatidylethanolamines, phosphatidylinositol, and sphingomyelin) did not change
significantly among the groups (Response Figures 9e-h).
We further used thin-layer chromatography (TLC) to determine the TG content in
the ER of each group. Compared with the IL-1β + NM-NTU + dark group, the IL-1β +
NM-NTU + light group contained more TGs (Response Figure 9i). To address whether
ER–mitochondria contact was related to TG levels, we modulated TG levels in the ER
by applying inhibitors of TG synthesis. The final and committed step of TG synthesis
is catalysed by two diacylglycerol acyltransferases, DGAT1 and DGAT2, which are
ER-resident transmembrane enzymes [PMID: 32559414]. We treated NPCs with a
DGAT1 inhibitor (A-922500) and a DGAT2 inhibitor (PF-06424439) or a combination
of both. TLC analysis of ER lipids confirmed that inhibiting DGAT1 and DGAT2,
either individually or in combination, reduced the TG levels in the ER (Response Figure 9j).
We then performed immunofluorescence experiments using calnexin and TOMM20 in
cells treated with DGAT1 and DGAT2 inhibitors. Compared with the control group, the
inhibition of TG synthesis significantly increased the number of mitochondrial–
endoplasmic reticulum contact sites (MERCS) (Response Figures 9k, l). These results
suggested a link between TG levels and the phenotype of MERCS. We further discuss
the reasons for this link. Since inhibition of TG synthesis disrupts the channelling of
fatty acids into neutral lipid storage [PMID: 28768178] and disruption of lipid
homeostasis elicits ER stress [PMID: 19966778], the formation of MERCS may
increase as an adaptive response to the unfolded protein response [PMID: 36586409,
33335290]. In general, our findings indicated that an altered ER lipidome (reduced TG
levels) might contribute to increased ER–mitochondria contact.
We subsequently analysed the acyl chain compositions of TG. Compared with
those in the IL-1β + NM-NTU + light group, the proportions of TG (50:2)[NL-18:1],
TG (54:2)[NL-18:0], TG (52:3)[NL-16:1], TG (56:3)[NL-18:1], and TG (54:3)[NL-
18:1] significantly increased (Response Figure 9m). The TG volcano map further
confirmed these results (Response Figure 9n). The proportion of unsaturated TG in the
IL-1β + NM-NTU + light group was significantly greater than that in the IL-1β + NM-
NTU + dark group (Response Figure 9o). In summary, NM-NTU + light treatment
increased the unsaturation levels of TGs. Given that lipid unsaturation significantly
increased membrane fluidity [PMID: 29410529] and affected the contact between
intracellular organelles [PMID: 36746962], we speculated that the NM-NTU reduced
the formation of MERCS in degenerative cells by enhancing membrane fluidity. Next,
we measured global membrane fluidity in NPCs using a membrane fluidity kit.
Membrane fluidity was quantified by measuring the ratio of excimer to monomer
fluorescence of lipophilic pyrene probes [PMID: 36103824]. With increasing
membrane fluidity, the probe underwent excimer formation. We found that NPCs in the
IL-1β + NM-NTU + light group exhibited greater membrane fluidity than did those in
the IL-1β + NM-NTU + dark group (Response Figure 9p). Overall, NM-NTUs with
light illumination might affect ER–mitochondria contact by remodelling the lipid
composition of the ER.

Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion. We fully agree
that direct measurement of cell viability is crucial for evaluating cellular status.
Therefore, we tested cell viability using 3-(4,5-dimethylthiazol-2-yl)-2,5-
diphenyltetrazolium bromide (MTT) and live/dead staining assays. In the MTT assay,
compared with that of normal NPCs, the viability of degenerated nucleus pulposus cells
(NPCs) decreased to 68.2% (Response Figure 12a). However, in the live/dead staining
assay, after the cells were incubated with calcein-AM/propidium iodide (PI), we
detected no significant difference in the percentage of live cells between the
degenerated NPCs and normal NPCs (Response Figure 12b, c).
We further attempted to determine the reasons for this difference. In the MTT assay,
the water-soluble yellow MTT dye is taken up by cells and reduced to purple formazan
by enzymes such as NAD(P)H-dependent oxidoreductase enzyme and mitochondrial
succinate dehydrogenase [PMID: 38593323]. The reduction in MTT occurs only in
metabolically active cells, and alterations in metabolic activity may lead to variations
in outcomes. Therefore, the lower absorbance (cell viability) shown in the MTT assay
of degenerated NPCs might be due to a decrease in cellular metabolic activity. In the
live/dead staining assay, although the cell viability of the degenerated NPCs decreased,
cell death did not occur (PI staining negative).
These findings suggested that although degenerated NPCs exhibited reduced
metabolic activity and viability, substantial cell death did not occur. These results were
also consistent with pathological changes in degenerated NPCs (such as altered Ca2+
levels, oxidative stress, and decreased mitochondrial membrane potential). We also
apologize for the spelling error and have corrected the misspelling of “degeneration” in
Figure 1. The labels are now accurate.

Response: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s insightful suggestions regarding the
MERCS quantification criteria. We agree that a precise, standardized definition and
robust sampling are essential for accurate interpretation. In response to this comment,
we have thoroughly revised our MERCS analysis protocol on the basis of established
methodologies [PMID: 36746962, 40514428]. ER–mitochondria contacts can be
characterized by gap distances, which are usually in the range from 10–80 nm,
with many focusing on 30 nm [PMID: 16982799, 30894536]. In accordance with a previous
study [PMID: 36746962], we defined contact sites as those with a tethered proximity
between membrane-bound organelles. The contacts were categorized and quantified
into three distinct ranges: ≤25 nm, 25<distance≤50 nm, and 50<distance≤100 nm. This
stratified approach allowed for a more nuanced and biologically relevant assessment of
changes in MERCS under different conditions. Quantitative analysis was performed on
a rigorously increased number of samples, with n = 3 independent biological replicates
per condition, encompassing a total of 50 cells and 63–65 randomly sampled fields of
view. For each field of view, we systematically quantified the ER tubules closely
apposed to the mitochondria, the number of mitochondria, and the average length of
the ER tubules. The details of the quantitative method are as follows. Briefly, the scale
of the image was set using the Set Scale tool in ImageJ. The length of the ER and the
perimeter of the mitochondria were subsequently measured using a freehand line tool.
The percent contact length was determined by taking the ratio of the length of the ER
(within contact distances of 0–100 nm) to the perimeter of the mitochondria.
The results revealed that compared with normal NPCs, degenerated NPCs
presented significant increased ER tubules closely apposed to mitochondria, indicating
increased formation of MERCS (Response Figure 14a, b). There was no significant
difference in the number of mitochondria or the average length of ER tubules between
normal NPCs and degenerated NPCs (Response Figure 14c, d). We believe these
methodological improvements, prompted by the reviewer's insightful comment,
provide a more robust and definitive quantification of MERCS and strengthen the
conclusions of our study.

Response: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comment regarding the
role of IL-1β in inducing NPC degeneration. As a key member of the IL-1 family, IL-
1β is widely recognized for its critical role in inflammation-related diseases [PMID:
30995499]. In the context of IVDD, IL-1β is considered a pivotal factor that amplifies
inflammatory cascades. Study has shown that IL-1β expression is significantly elevated
in degenerative intervertebral discs and that this cytokine is involved in multiple
pathological processes associated with IVDD [PMID: 17688691]. Moreover, increased
IL-1β synthesis accelerated degenerative changes in IVDD [PMID: 37088216].
Furthermore, studies have used IL-1β to induce NPC degeneration, which may be
related to its ability to increase the expression of matrix degradation-related genes
(MMP3, MMP13, and ADAMTS-4) and decrease the expression of matrix synthesis-
related genes (ACAN and COL2A1), resulting in an imbalance between catabolic and
anabolic events in NPCs [PMID: 35984761, 15987475, 32583517]. Therefore, the IL-
1β exposure model serves not only as a simulation of inflammation but also as a well-
established system for investigating pathological processes in NPC degeneration. We
have revised the manuscript and added these citations to clarify these points and ensure
a more precise description of the model’s relevance to IVDD.

inhibiting glycolysis [PMID: 25218591].

Comment-10: “Do NTUs also generate a signal to stimulate ATP production by
endogeneous mitochondria? Can ATP generated from NTUs alone produce the
therapeutic effect?”
Response: Regarding the second part of the question, degenerative NPCs are
characterized by a disruption in the mitochondria–endoplasmic reticulum interaction
network. We hypothesized that the ATP produced by NM-NTUs in this context played
a crucial signalling role, helping to remodel and restore the homeostasis of this
dysfunctional interorganellar network. In turn, this process might restore endogenous
mitochondria, enabling them to resume their normal ATP-generating function.
To investigate whether NM-NTU treatment led to increased ATP production from
endogenous mitochondria in degenerated NPCs, we transfected cells with a genetically
encoded mitochondrial ATP indicator (mit-AT1.03) to measure changes in
mitochondrial ATP concentrations65-67. The ratio of yellow fluorescence protein (YFP)
to cyan fluorescence protein (CFP) was measured by flow cytometry to determine the
mitochondrial ATP level. The results showed that following NM-NTUs + light
treatment, the mitochondria within degenerated NPCs produced more ATP compared
with the IL-1β group (Response Figures 20a, b). These results indicated that NM-NTUs
might stimulate endogenous mitochondria in degenerated NPCs to produce ATP. In
conclusion, while the NTUs themselves produced a quantifiable amount of ATP, a key
therapeutic mechanism was that the NTU-generated ATP acted as a signal to restore the
homeostasis of organelle interaction networks and promote the energy production of
endogenous mitochondria.

synthesis significantly increased the number of MERCS (Response Figure 25c, d).

further discussed the reasons for this link. Since inhibition of TG synthesis disrupted
the channelling of fatty acids into neutral lipid storage [PMID: 28768178] and
disruption of lipid homeostasis elicited ER stress [PMID: 19966778], the formation of
MERCS might increase as an adaptive response to the unfolded protein response
[PMID: 36586409, 33335290]. In general, our findings indicated that an altered ER
lipidome (reduced TG levels) might contribute to increased ER–mitochondria contact.

Comment-21: “-How are Line 47 & 48 related to mitochondria acquisition from Line
49?”
Response: We thank the reviewer for the valuable comment. We have strengthened the
description of the relationship between life evolution and mitochondrial acquisition.
According to the timeline of life evolution, approximately 3.5 billion years ago,
DNA/protein-containing organisms evolved into cyanobacteria [PMID: 8681375,
15073369]. According to molecular phylogeny and biogeochemistry studies,
eukaryotes appeared approximately 1.5 billion years ago [PMID: 11452306]. The origin
and cellular complexity of eukaryotes represent a major enigma in biology. Current data
support scenarios in which an archaeal host cell and an alphaproteobacterial
(mitochondrial) endosymbiont merged together, resulting in the first eukaryotic cell
[PMID: 28077874]. Research has shown that all complex life is composed of eukaryotic
cells. Eukaryotic cells arising from prokaryotes and otherwise prokaryotes show no
tendency to evolve greater complexity [PMID: 20962839]. The main reason for this
phenomenon is the energetics of genome complexity. The prokaryotic genome size is
constrained by bioenergetics. The acquisition of mitochondria in eukaryotes was a
revolution in cell structure. The endosymbiosis that gave rise to mitochondria
restructured the distribution of DNA in relation to bioenergetic membranes, permitting
a remarkable expansion in the number of genes that were expressed [PMID: 32428484].
In reality, mitochondrial power probably enabled an expansion in eukaryotic genome
size (from a maximum of 13 Mb in bacteria up to ∼150,000 Mb in eukaryotes), an
increase in the number of protein-coding genes (4-fold on average) and an increase in
gene expression of hundreds to thousands of times [PMID: 32428484]. This vast
increase in genomic capacity was strictly dependent on mitochondrial power and was a
prerequisite for eukaryotic complexity, the key innovation en route to multicellular life.
Action: To clarify this relationship, we have revised the relevant content in the
manuscript (Page 2).
“The early evolution of life underwent a process of formation from simple organic
molecules to precellular and primitive lives1,2. For the evolution of complex life, the
acquisition of mitochondria in eukaryotes is a prerequisite3,4. The endosymbiosis that
gave rise to mitochondria restructured the distribution of DNA in relation to
bioenergetic membranes, thereby allowing eukaryotes to significantly increase the
number of gene expressed compared with prokaryotes, based on which the diversity
and complexity of life have evolved4,5.”
Comment-22: “-How are malic acid cycle and energy homeostasis from Line 53 & 54
related to defensive adaptation mentioned in Line 52?”
Response: We thank the reviewer for the insightful comment. The reviewer raises an
important point regarding the connection between the malic acid cycle (malate valve)
and energy homeostasis on the one hand, and defensive adaptation on the other.
Malate valves are systems for balancing the ATP/NAD(P)H ratio required in
various subcellular compartments in plant cells. For energy-consuming reactions, the
delivery of NAD(P)H and ATP must take place at the required rates and in specific
compartments, since the pool sizes of these energy carriers are rather limited and, in
general, they are not directly transported across biomembranes [PMID: 15032873].
Plant cells possess specific translocators enabling the indirect exchange of reducing
equivalents. These translocators enable the exchange of dicarboxylates such as malate
and oxaloacetate (malate/OAA shuttles; Response Figure 32) [PMID: 29933514].
Malate is a versatile compound involved in plant metabolism that can easily be
transported across subcellular membranes and utilised as a substrate for mitochondrial
ATP production or for the provision of NADH to the cytosol (Response Figure 32).
Malate/OAA shuttles act in combination with malate dehydrogenases (MDHs) as key
enzymes connecting compartments. They are powerful systems for balancing metabolic
fluxes by enabling the indirect transfer of reducing equivalents and play a key role in
plant metabolism.
Therefore, the malate valve is a crucial regulatory mechanism that helps plants
maintain metabolic stability (energy homeostasis) under fluctuating or stressful
environmental conditions—which is, in itself, a fundamental defensive adaptation
[PMID: 15032873]. Plants are frequently exposed to rapid changes in environmental
conditions. The imposed changes can occur within seconds, minutes, hours or days.
At all instants, metabolism should run smoothly without major disturbances, and
metabolite pools should be kept constant. Clearly, regulation at various sites and levels
is required to achieve homeostasis of all metabolic fluxes and pools, particularly those
connected with the generation and consumption of reducing equivalents and ATP. The
various forms of energy should consistently be available at certain rates, at defined
ratios, such as those of NADPH to ATP, and in the various compartments according to
actual needs. The malate valve is a useful means to balance the ATP/NADPH ratio in
chloroplasts. Export of excess NAD(P)H through the malate valves will allow for the
continued production of ATP in photosynthesis and in oxidative phosphorylation. When
plants are subjected to conditions such as high light, high CO , NH + nutrition, and cold
2 4
stress, which require altered activity of malate valve enzymes, altered expression levels
of the MDH isoforms can be observed to balance the cellular reducing equivalents
[PMID: 15032873, 29933514, 22140244].
Action: To clarify this point, we have modified the manuscript to directly present both
the malate valve and the maintenance of energy homeostasis as integral components of
the plant’s defensive adaptation to stress (Pages 2-3).
“Plants possess mitochondria and chloroplasts and exhibit unique defensive adaptations
to stress6,7. Malate/oxaloacetate translocators together with malate dehydrogenases
(malate valves) connect chloroplasts and mitochondria in plant cells. When plants are
subjected to conditions such as high light, high CO , and cold stress, the activities of
2
the enzymes of the malate valves change to balance the ATP/NAD(P)H ratio required
in subcellular compartments and therefore balance metabolic fluxes under stress
conditions8-10.”

Comment-23: “-Line 55 & 56: Is changing the unsaturation of the membrane lipids
related to mitochondrial or chloroplastic functions? If yes, add a few words to explain
their role in this process to make connection with Line 52 ‘defensive adaptation by
mitochondria and chloroplast’”
Response: We thank the reviewer for the valuable suggestion. Changes in membrane
lipid unsaturation are related to the functions of chloroplasts. Generally, membrane
fluidity is affected by changes in temperature, with the most common response to
chilling being an increase in fatty acid unsaturation in membrane lipids. This
phenomenon enables the membranes to maintain their functional fluidity and is
essential for plant survival during cold stress [PMID: 15519313, 27835850, 23585650,
11607410]. The ω3 fatty acid desaturase FAD8 is localized in chloroplasts and is
responsible for trienoic fatty acid production in plants [PMID: 16930600, 12232435].
The FAD8 gene was identified as a cold-inducible temperature-sensitive ω3 desaturase.
In Arabidopsis and maize, the overall level of FAD8 mRNA is elevated at relatively low
temperatures [PMID: 7846164, 9484441], indicating the connection between
chloroplast-localized FAD8 and fatty acid desaturation in cold environments.
Action: We have revised the manuscript to clarify this mechanistic connection (Page
3).
“The increase in fatty acid unsaturation in membrane lipids enables the membranes to
maintain their functional fluidity and is essential for plants to survive during cold
stress11-14. To adapt to chilling or freezing temperatures, plants can utilise chloroplast-
localized fatty acid desaturase (FAD8) to alter the unsaturation of membrane lipids. The
cold-inducible ω3 fatty acid desaturase FAD8 is responsible for trienoic fatty acid
production in plants15,16. In Arabidopsis and maize, the overall level of FAD8 mRNA is
elevated at relatively low temperatures17,18, indicating the connection between
chloroplast-localized FAD8 and fatty acid desaturation in cold environments.”

highlighting the role of the mitochondria-associated ER membrane (MAM) in lipid
metabolism in the Introduction would strengthen the background of the manuscript.
The endoplasmic reticulum (ER) dedicates a special domain for metabolic
interactions with mitochondria and is referred to as the mitochondria-associated ER
membrane (MAM) [PMID: 22575682]. MAM plays important roles in various cellular
functions, including acting as a tight platform for lipid synthesis and lipid transfer
between the ER and mitochondria [PMID: 22575682, 19144519]. The lipid metabolism
function of the MAM has been well characterized. MAM is enriched in lipid
metabolism-related enzymes, such as phosphatidylserine synthase,
phosphatidylethanolamine methyltransferase-2, acyl-CoA:cholesterol acyltransferase,
and diacylglycerol acyltransferase [PMID: 19144519].

Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. Linear electron transport
in the thylakoid membrane drives photosynthetic energy (ATP) and reduces equivalent
(NADPH) production [PMID: 31245694]. Therefore, in addition to their role in energy
production, NTUs may also contribute to cellular metabolism through the generation of
NADPH, which plays a critical role in redox homeostasis [PMID: 36477541,
28514672]. NADPH is used as a cofactor by glutathione reductase to reduce oxidized
glutathione (GSSG→2GSH) and, likewise, by thioredoxin reductase to reduce oxidized
thioredoxin. Both of these molecules contribute to defence against oxidative stress
[PMID: 36505922, 19451637].
We further explored this role experimentally. First, we evaluated the effects of NM-
NTUs + light on the regulation of intracellular NADPH levels. The results revealed that
compared with that in the control NPCs, the NADPH content in the IL-1β-induced
degenerated NPCs was decreased. Compared with the IL-1β + NM-NTUs + dark
treatment, the IL-1β + NM-NTUs + light treatment significantly restored cellular
NADPH levels (Response Figure 33a). Furthermore, by using a reactive oxygen species
(ROS) assay kit, we found that the IL-1β + NM-NTUs + light group had reduced
intracellular ROS levels compared with the IL-1β + NM-NTUs + dark group (Response
Figures 33b, c). These findings support the conclusion that, in addition to producing
energy, NTUs may also help to mitigate cellular oxidative stress through the generation
of NADPH.
ROS play major roles in inducing the ER stress response. Study has shown that
ROS originating from the ER and mitochondria disturb ER protein folding and generate
ER stress [PMID: 33558590]. Booth et al. demonstrated that the ER-mitochondrial
interface hosts a nanodomain of H O originating from mitochondrial cristae [PMID:
2 2
27397688]. Another study revealed that high mitochondrial ROS levels promote MAM
formation and are associated with MAM-ROS and ER-ROS bursts [PMID: 41032619].
Therefore, we hypothesize that NADPH produced by NTUs may indirectly affect the
contact between mitochondria and the ER through the regulation of redox homeostasis.

Comment-30: “-Lines 231-241: Make a better transition to justify the investigation of
ER lipid composition. Add references regarding the connection between membrane
fluidity to MAM.”
Response: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comment. ER‐localized
enzymes synthesize the vast majority of cellular lipids. The ER has a major influence
on cellular lipid biomass and membrane biogenesis and balances the production of
different lipid categories, classes, and species [PMID: 29074503]. ER membrane lipid
composition is altered in response to stressful conditions. For example, under prolonged
nutrient and oxidative stress, the ER membrane lipid composition is remodelled to
involve an increased proportion of saturated phospholipids that are less susceptible to
oxidation [PMID: 38395735]. Moreover, the acyl chain saturation of membrane lipids
is crucial for membrane fluidity, with unsaturated lipid acyl chains enabling better
fluidity and saturated lipid acyl chains forming nonfluid and packed structures [PMID:
37652754, 29410529].
With respect to the connection between membrane fluidity and MAM, the study
showed that the loss of the p97-UBXD8 complex increased the number of
mitochondrial–ER contact sites (MERCS) by reducing membrane lipid unsaturation
and global membrane fluidity [PMID: 36746962]. UBXD8 KO cells exhibited greater
abundances of PCs, PEs, DGs, and TG lipids with saturated fatty acyl tails, leading to
decreased global membrane fluidity, which in turn resulted in increased MERCS. This
aberrant contact phenotype could be rescued by unsaturated fatty acid supplementation.
In summary, Ganji et al. reported that increased membrane saturation leading to loss of
fluidity may affect the dynamic association and disassociation between organelles,
further leading to an increase in MERCS.
Therefore, we investigated the lipidome of the ER to assess the relationships among
ER lipid composition, membrane fluidity, and ER–mitochondria contact, as well as the
regulatory role of NM-NTUs in this process.

Response: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comment. We understand
the reviewer’s concern that in vitro culture may alter the phenotype of nucleus pulposus
cells (NPCs) isolated from degenerated intervertebral discs. Studies have explored
methods for isolating and culturing NPCs to yield the greatest number of cells and
maintain viability and phenotype as close to those observed in vivo as possible [PMID:
25749011, 19953600, 36994456]. These studies found that gene expression patterns in
human NPCs were substantially affected by passage number/culture time. When the
cell culture reached passage 2 (approximately 11–13 days), the NPCs showed
significant changes in the expression of phenotypic markers (such as KRT18, CD24,
and COL2A1).
In our study, we obtained degenerated human NPCs from deteriorated
intervertebral disc tissue. Since the number of NPCs obtained directly from tissue
digestion is limited (approximately 104 to 105 per gram of tissue [PMID: 36994456]),
which is insufficient for subsequent experiments, we cultured the NPCs in vitro for 5
days. On the basis of previous reports, the phenotype of human NPCs only changes
significantly after approximately 11–13 days of in vitro culture [PMID: 25749011,
36994456]; therefore, we chose a 5-day culture time to reduce the impact of phenotypic
changes on subsequent experiments.
To further evaluate the effects of 5 days of in vitro culture on the phenotypic
changes in degenerated human NPCs, we monitored the phenotypic profiles of
degenerated human NPCs cultured for 1–9 days. Referring to previous studies [PMID:
25749011, 36994456], we examined the following NPC phenotypic markers: genes
(CD24, KRT18, KRT19, SOX9, MIA, FN1, COL1A1, COL2A1, and COL3A1) and
proteins (CD24 and KRT19). The results indicated that the gene and protein phenotypes
of the degenerated NPCs remained stable during the first 5 days of culture, whereas
changes in the expression of certain markers began to emerge on day 7 (Response
Figure 1a, b). Specifically, the gene expression of CD24 increased on both day 7 and
day 9. The expression of KRT18, KRT19, SOX9, and MIA genes increased on day 7 but
decreased on day 9. Furthermore, the expression of FN1 gene decreased on day 9. The
expression of COL1A1, COL2A1, and COL3A1 genes decreased on day 7. On day 9,
the expression of COL1A1 and COL3A1 genes was upregulated, while that of COL2A1
was further downregulated (Response Figure 1a). The changes in the abundance of
CD24 and KRT19 proteins over culture time tended to be similar to the changes in gene
expression (Response Figure 1b). In summary, these results indicate that NPCs
extracted from degenerated nucleus pulposus tissue maintained a stable phenotype for
5 days in culture but exhibited phenotypic changes and instability after 7 days of culture.
Therefore, the 5-day in vitro culture time selected in this study did not significantly alter
the phenotype of degenerated human NPCs.

Comment-2: “2.Why does the Dil fluorescence appear in the nucleus in the Figure
3i?”
Response: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s careful observation of the DiI
fluorescence signal in the nucleus shown in Figure 3i. We apologize for the lack of
clarity in our previous explanation. To address this concern, we repeated the experiment
and provided three-dimensional images as well as cross-sectional images. Three-
dimensional reconstruction revealed that some NTUDiI (NTUs labelled with DiI) were
positioned above the nucleus (Response Figure 2a). Confocal laser scanning
microscopy (CLSM) uses pinholes to eliminate out-of-focus emissions, achieving
optical sectioning (Response Figure 2b) [PMID: 29927100]. When tiny spheres are
being imaged, the light passing through the optical system undergoes diffraction,
resulting in a point source image that is much larger than the actual size of the object.
Diffraction causes light to spread along the lateral and axial optical axes of the
microscope, with the axial image plane more pronounced [PMID: 22082987]. A smaller
pinhole can minimize diffraction rings and improve resolution, whereas a larger pinhole
can receive more light and enhance contrast. There is a trade-off between these two
factors [PMID: 31876974]. In our earlier experiments, we used a larger pinhole size,
which led to the projection of NTUDiI located above or below the nucleus onto the
nuclear plane (Response Figure 2c). We found that when pinholes of an appropriate size
were used, NTUDiI did not localize to the nucleus (Response Figure 2d). However, with
a slightly larger pinhole, the fluorescence from the same NTUDiI appeared to overlap
with that of the nucleus in the cross-sectional view of the same cell (Response Figure
2e). Therefore, we conclude that the previous image was an artefact and not nuclear
localization of the NTUs. In our initial submission, we used a larger pinhole size, which
caused artefacts because of overlapping fluorescence signals during imaging. We
sincerely apologize for this. To resolve this issue, we repeated the experiment, used a
suitable pinhole size, and replaced the original image with a clearer, more representative
image in which no NTUDiI fluorescence was detected in the cell nucleus (Response
Figure 3a). Moreover, the results indicated that the cell membrane coating enabled the
NTUs to bypass lysosomal degradation (Response Figure 3a, b).
